title: How to Eat Dinner Together Again
excerpt: The shared table is where a family is built or quietly lost. Most homes did not decide to stop eating together. They drifted, one busy night at a time.
body:
No family decides to stop eating together. It happens by erosion. A practice swallows one night, then another. The schedule fills, the kids scatter to their rooms, someone eats in the car, and within a few years the family has gathered around a shared table maybe twice a week, and no one chose it. The common meal, which every generation before ours treated as the ordinary center of home life, has quietly become an occasion.

This matters more than it looks. The shared table is not a sentimental nicety. It is the place where a family does most of its actual forming, the daily ground where children are heard, where conflicts surface and settle, where faith gets talked about in the cracks between passing the salt. Lose the table and you do not just lose a meal. You lose the room where the family was being made.

## Why the table carries so much weight

The meal sits near the center of the Christian story for a reason. Jesus was forever at tables, eating with the wrong people, scandalizing the careful by who he broke bread with. On the last night, he gave his disciples a meal to remember him by, not a lecture and not a book. A table. The deepest things in our faith are tied to eating together, because God knows what a shared meal does to people who would otherwise stay strangers.

A family at a table is a family that cannot easily hide from one another. The phone goes down, the faces turn in, and over weeks and years the small daily exposure does its slow work. The child who eats with their parents most nights is, by every measure we have, steadier, safer, and more anchored. This is not magic. It is the simple force of being known, repeated daily.

## Start by deciding it is non-negotiable

The table will not survive if it is optional, because something will always be more urgent. So the first move is a decision, made out loud, that the family eats together on a set number of nights and those nights are protected. Not every night, if that is impossible. But a real number, defended against the next thing that wants to take it. Activities that cannot fit around the table get reconsidered, not the other way around.

This will cost you. It means saying no to good things, declining the schedule everyone else accepts. Do it anyway. You are not protecting a meal. You are protecting the place your children are formed.

## Keep the table simple and unhurried

The meal does not have to be elaborate. A simple dinner eaten slowly beats an impressive one eaten in shifts. The aim is not the food. It is the time, the lingering, the conversation that only happens when no one is rushing to leave. So resist the urge to clear and scatter the moment the eating is done. The best things at a table are often said after the plates are empty, when there is no task left but to be together.

Put the phones somewhere else. All of them, parents included. A table with a screen on it is not a shared table; it is several people eating near each other. The face-to-face is the whole point, and a glowing rectangle defeats it instantly.

## Bring God to the table without forcing it

Begin with grace, every time, even when it is rushed and rote. The simple act of stopping to thank God before eating teaches a child that the food is a gift and the day is held by someone. Then let faith come up naturally in the talk, not as a scheduled segment but in the ordinary flow. A question a child asks. A hard thing that happened. The day's small troubles handed, in passing, to God.

The table is also where family worship most naturally lives. When the meal is ending and everyone is still seated, read a few verses, say a sentence, pray. You do not need a separate occasion. The table you already keep is the altar you already have.

## Repair the practice without shame

If your family has drifted, do not begin with a guilt-soaked speech about how you have all failed. Just start. Pick the nights. Sit down. The children will adjust faster than you fear, especially the younger ones, and even the teenager who groans will, in time, come to count on it. The table is not rebuilt by remorse. It is rebuilt by sitting down, tonight, and again tomorrow.

I have let the table erode in my own home, busy with good and necessary things, telling myself it was a season. Seasons become years. The recovery did not come from feeling bad about it. It came from putting the meal back on the calendar and defending it like it mattered, because it did.

## This week

Name the number of nights your family will eat together this week and write them down. Defend them against the next thing that asks for them. Put every phone in another room. Begin with grace. Eat slowly and stay seated a little longer than feels efficient. Before everyone rises, read a few verses and pray for one real thing.

Do it again next week. The table is not built in an evening. It is built by the unremarkable act of sitting down together, night after night, until your children cannot imagine home without it.
